newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico Cactus natgas output still off 50 pct-Pemex.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Cactus natgas output still off 50 pct-Pemex.

text.p: Mexico's largest natural gas processing complex was still running at less than half its capacity in February after last July's explosion at the site, according to a document obtained from state oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex).
The explosion at the Cactus complex in southern Chiapas state destroyed two processing plants and severly crimped capacity, requiring higher natural gas imports for months.
Final natural gas processing of sweet gas at Cactus in February totaled 605.96 million cubic feet per day (cfd) compared with 1.357 billion cfd in the same month last year, the report said.
Despite the minimal capacity change in the seven months since the July 26 blast, Pemex officials have said they expect a quick recovery to recoup the remaining half of capacity by June.
Processing of sweet gas was wiped out by about 75 percent of capacity after the blast, down to 332.42 million cfd in August from 1.304 billion cfd the year before.

Sweet gas is processed to remove excess liquids and produce natural gas, also known as methane. The complex also has a plant to remove sulphur through a sweetening process for sour gas, which must then be processed to final natural gas.

The complex's sour processing plant was less damaged than its sweet processing one, with sour output at 1.179 billion cfd in February compared with 1.292 billion cfd the year before, according to the report.
Mexico's associated natural gas, extracted along with crude, has a high sulphur content.
Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous said last year that Cactus natural gas processing would recover pre-blast capacity of 1.4 billion cfd by June 1997.
The explosion forced Mexico to import 300 million cfd in natural gas for the month following the blast. Pemex has also turned to Saudi Arabia for contracts to provide needed methane and propane.

Despite the Cactus explosion, Mexico's natural gas processing reached its highest level in four years at an average 3.324 bln cfd in 1996. Natural gas processing in the first two months of 1997 have also been on the rise.
Pemex officials said following the blast the company would compensate for lost processing capacity at Cactus by boosting capacity at other plants.

Cactus's ethane production in February was 20,090 barrels per day (bpd), down from 33,700 bpd the year before, according to the Pemex report. The ethane processing plant halted output for two months after July's blast.
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) capacity at the complex was 43,210 bpd in February, still down from 66,600 bpd during the same month in 1995.

The cost of lost production and repairs at the Cactus state explosion reached almost $200 million, Lajous has said. A Pemex employee was found to have left a valve open which caused the gas leakage that led to the blast that killed six Pemex employees.
Reconstruction work on the complex was contracted to ICA Fluor Daniel, a joint venture between Empresas ICA and Fluor Daniel GTI Inc, and was scheduled to be completed in April.
